preamble: The back-gliding diphthong /au/ became the front diphthong /ɛi/ in Faroese. At the beginning of the 14th century a delabialization affected the Old Norse rounded vowels and diphthongs, giving y, øy, au > /i, ɔi, ɛi/; Old Norse au thus has a reflex distinct from that of øy. Modern Faroese spells the result ey, pronounced [ɛiː] when long. No comparable direct au > ei change is well documented outside this branch, so the shift is rare.

examples.note: Old Norse au corresponds regularly to Faroese ey, pronounced [ɛi].

sources: Árnason, K. (2011). The Phonology of Icelandic and Faroese. Oxford University Press. https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199229314.001.0001
